To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people are more likely to justify inequality when they perceive that inequality to be legitimate; (2) people’s perceptions of legitimacy of inequality depend on the extent to which they believe that inequality is deserved and that it is necessary to maintain the status quo; (3) people’s perceptions that inequality is legitimate are more strongly related to their attitudes toward inequality when people are high rather than low in social dominance orientation and when people are high, rather than low, in system justification.

the legitimacy of inequality is a multidimensional construct, that it is related to the endorsement of inequality, that it is associated with the acceptance of the status quo, that it can be predicted by a number of individual and group-level factors, and that it can have a number of different consequences.
The legitimacy of social inequality is an important factor in determining whether people support or resist it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how social psychological processes contribute to the maintenance of social inequality.
the social psychological underpinnings of the legitimation of inequalities in society, and the consequences of these processes for individuals, groups and society at large.
understanding the social processes by which people come to view and justify the differential distribution of resources, opportunities and outcomes in a society.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no one single theory that can explain all the aspects of the legitimation of inequality.
the legitimation of inequality is a complex and multi-level process that is embedded in social, cultural and historical context.
social psychological theories and research on legitimation have contributed greatly to the understanding of the processes underlying the acceptance and maintenance of social inequality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the research presented in this issue provides a strong foundation for future research and interventions aimed at reducing social inequality.
social psychology has made great progress in understanding how social inequalities are maintained and legitimated.

we have shown the importance of understanding the social context in which social inequality is embedded and the importance of understanding how people’s social identities and social group memberships shape their perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors in ways that can perpetuate social inequality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the legitimation of inequality is a process that occurs at multiple levels and that it can be influenced by multiple interventions.
people can hold multiple and even conflicting attitudes about the same social group at the same time, and that these attitudes can change depending on the context.
people are not passive recipients of the social world.
